Coating Challenges for Metal Fabricators and Welding Shops

The main coating challenges for fabricators are weld seams, spatter, mixed metal thickness, sharp edges and tight deadlines. Each can cause thin spots, pinholes or rework without planning. Powder coating for metal fabricators works best when the weld is treated as part of the finish.

Welds are rough and often porous, and they heat differently from the sheet beside them. Weld spatter leaves bumps that show through the coating. Weld porosity traps air, which oven heat can push out as outgassing and leave blisters. Sharp edges pull the coating thin, so edge coverage needs attention on cut plate and tube ends. A heavy base plate welded to thin sheet also heats unevenly in the oven. Add the deadlines your own customers set, and finishing often becomes the bottleneck. Good powder coating for fabricators removes these risks before parts reach the oven, which keeps fabricated metal parts moving. Fabricator powder coating also has to cope with mixed shapes, sizes and metals, often in the same batch.
Choosing powder coating for metal fabricators with a documented prep routine protects your reputation as well as the part, because a failed finish comes back to the shop that built the frame.

How We Work With Fabrication Shops

Powder coating for metal fabricators follows five stages at Koojo: intake and inspection, cleaning and pretreatment, masking and powder application, oven curing, and final inspection. We document each stage so repeat runs follow the same steps, and typical orders follow a 48-hour turnaround.
Step 1 – Intake and Inspection

We inspect each part for spatter, oil, rust, old coatings and damage, and we agree the finish and timing with you. Photos sent before drop-off help us flag issues early. Planning how a welded frame will hang comes first, because every surface must be reachable.
Step 2 – Cleaning and Pretreatment

Parts are cleaned and pretreated chemically so the powder can bond to bare metal. Early coating failures often trace back to weak cleaning, so powder coating for welded parts is never treated as a spray-only job. Residue collects along weld seams, so those areas get close attention.
Step 3 – Masking and Powder Application

We plug threaded holes and cover mating faces first. The powder is then sprayed electrostatically onto the grounded part, which draws it around tube walls and corners. Deep recesses can limit coverage, so racking and spray angles are planned in advance.
Step 4 – Oven Curing
Parts cure in the oven at 180 to 200 °C. Heavy base plates take longer to reach temperature than thin sheet, so fabricator powder coating schedules each assembly by its mass.
Step 5 – Final Inspection and Handoff
The cured finish is checked for coverage, adhesion and appearance. We log the colour code and powder so a later run can match, and parts are received Monday to Friday, 7 AM to 5 PM.

For shops with recurring work, this routine supports batch consistency from one run to the next. If your shop sends parts weekly, say so at quote and we will plan around it. Powder Coating for Metal Fabricators FAQs

Short answer: powder coating for metal fabricators works best when prep, thickness and timing are agreed up front. These answers cover welds, tolerances, timing and logistics for welded and fabricated parts, so you know what to expect before you send work.

blocks.q: Should we grind welds before sending parts?
blocks.a: Grind off heavy spatter and sharp burrs where you can, because they show through the finish. Smooth, sealed welds also cure better, which makes powder coating for metal fabricators more predictable. Tell us what you have already done, and our team inspects the rest at intake.

blocks.q: Why do some welds bubble after curing?
blocks.a: Air or residue trapped in a porous weld can escape as heat rises, which leaves a blister or pinhole. Sealing welds before coating lowers the risk. Mention porous sections at quote, and we plan the cure around them, which is routine in powder coating for fabrication shops.

blocks.q: Can you coat parts with tight tolerances?
blocks.a: Yes. Coating thickness affects fit, so flag threaded holes, bores and fit-critical parts when you request a quote. Powder coating for metal fabrication can work with tight fits when we know where they are, so we mask those areas before coating.

blocks.q: Do you take subcontract work from other shops?
blocks.a: Yes. We take subcontract powder coating from fabrication and welding shops, and we record the colour code and powder on each job. Ask about outsourced powder coating for recurring work at quote.

blocks.q: Can steel and aluminum parts go in the same order?
blocks.a: Yes, mixed metals can be quoted together, but each metal gets its own prep and cure plan. List the metal for every part when you request a quote.

blocks.q: What should we send with a quote request?
blocks.a: Send photos, dimensions, quantities, the metal and your finish choice. Drawings and part counts help us plan racking. With those details, powder coating for welding shops can be quoted and scheduled faster, and we flag any prep concerns before parts arrive.
